Someone's point-of-view is based on a number of things, age being just one of them. I am a firm believer that in general, people really start to observe the greater world around them when they are 8 - 12 years old. They end up having a greater affinity or attachment to the world at that time; it's like that's when their world view begins.

For example, you may have seen those birthday cards that show what the world was like when you were born. I saw the card for my birth year and I could not relate to it at all. The card showed what song/TV show was popular that year, what car was popular that year, perhaps how much a gallon of milk or gas cost, as well as a bunch of other key cultural events/metrics/toys. None of it resonated. I saw the cards that reflected 8 to 12 years after my birth year and it resonated a lot more.

Tying this together, someone's understanding of an event or idea depends a lot on how old they were when the event took place or the idea became popular. As an example, most high school seniors going on to college today would have been toddlers/young children when the September 11th attacks took place; more to the point, they probably have no real understanding of what the world was like before then. They might know from reading about it, but they would not understand it from living it. Those same seniors have a different understanding of the internet than say middle-aged people - not just in the obvious difference that the younger people would be more technologically savvy, but more so in how younger people relate to the internet. Flipping those two groups around, you could say that middle-aged people have a stronger attachment to cars than younger people.

Tl;dr Yes, but for me it's not so much an age thing as a what have you experienced in your lifetime and at what times (especially in your formative years) that shapes your understanding of the world.
